title: Something new (Berakhot 29b)
hookLine: prayer said as a fixed burden isn't a plea; add something new
tomorrow: they waited before they prayed. what were they waiting for?

cards: A favorite song on repeat goes flat eventually. You still know every word; you've just stopped hearing them. So here's a puzzle in Berakhot.
The Amidah has set words, said every day. Yet the Mishnah warns: whoever makes their prayer keva, fixed, their prayer isn't a plea. A fixed prayer that mustn't be fixed.

teach.b: The Talmud asks the obvious question: what does fixed mean here? And it gives three answers. In Rabbi Oshaya's name: fixed is when your prayer feels like a heavy load, something to get off your back.

The Rabbis say: fixed is when you don't say it as a plea, when it's recited instead of asked. And Rabba and Rav Yosef say: fixed is when you can't add something new in it. Put them together and the puzzle solves itself.
Keva isn't about the words being set.
It's about the person saying them. A burden, a recitation, a rerun: that's what goes stale. The cure is small.
Something new each time. And then the Talmud does something kind.

teach.h: RABBI ZEIRA: I MIGHT LOSE MY PLACE.
teach.b: In the same passage, Rabbi Zeira admits he could add something new, but he's afraid he'll lose his place. Even the sages found this hard, and said so.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight. In this passage, the test of a living prayer isn't whether the words are old. It's whether you brought one new thing to them today.

how: Jewish prayer keeps set words, and the halakhic tradition allows a person to add personal requests in fitting places in the Amidah, so the same prayer can carry something new each day.

o: change the order of the prayers every morning
bring one fresh thing to words you say every day
write a whole new prayer to replace the old one

games.q: three kinds of 'fixed' — tap the pairs.

s: keva means a prayer's words must never stay the same
the Amidah's words are set; keva is a prayer said as a burden, not asked, or with nothing new.
one sage admits adding something new might make him lose his place
Rabbi Zeira says it in the same passage.
the Talmud gives just one definition of 'fixed'
it gives three: a heavy load, recited not asked, nothing new.

games.q: your friend plays the same piano piece at every recital and says it feels dead now. using Berakhot 29b, what would help?
o: keep the piece, and bring one new thing to it each time.
drop the piece; once something repeats, it's dead for good.
play it faster, so it's over before it gets heavy.
games.why: the Talmud doesn't throw out set words. Rabba and Rav Yosef: what's fixed is a prayer you can't add something new to.

practice: Pick a line you already know by heart: a blessing, a verse, a sentence you say every day. Say it out loud, slowly, then add one word or phrase of your own that's true today. Say it once more with the new part in it.

wordCard.voice: Something new. Berakhot's cure for keva: set words are fine, as long as you bring one new thing to them each time.

orig.note: Hebrew: fixed, set. the Mishnah's word for a prayer that has gone stale.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: something new each time, even inside the oldest words. Twenty of fifty in Berakhot.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 and Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 29b (one who makes his prayer keva; three definitions; Rabbi Zeira's worry)
